title: Content Safety and Moderation
learning_outcomes: Explain content policy design and how it connects to content safety and moderation.
Apply input and output moderation in the example and predict the output before running it.
Test one realistic edge case for content safety and moderation and explain what the example does not prove.

content.intro: This lesson covers content safety and moderation through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Defend the entire system—not just the prompt—against injection, data leakage, unsafe outputs, unauthorized actions, and supply-chain risks.
content.why_it_matters: Content policy design requires a documented decision that fits the use case and jurisdiction. Identify affected stakeholders, distinguish binding obligations from voluntary guidance, retain evidence for the decision, and revisit the conclusion when the model, data, product, or applicable rules change.

items.title: Content policy design
items.text: Content policy design requires a documented decision that fits the use case and jurisdiction. Identify affected stakeholders, distinguish binding obligations from voluntary guidance, retain evidence for the decision, and revisit the conclusion when the model, data, product, or applicable rules change.

items.title: Input and output moderation
items.text: Input and output moderation is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

items.title: Risk-based moderation strategies
items.text: Risk-based moderation strategies is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

items.title: Handling ambiguous or borderline requests
items.text: Handling ambiguous or borderline requests belongs to the application integration boundary. Validate inputs before sending them, keep credentials on the server, handle non-success responses and cancellation, and log request metadata without storing secrets or unnecessary personal content. Provider-specific payloads must be checked against the selected API's current documentation.

items.title: False positives and false negatives
items.text: Use false positives and false negatives as a lens for understanding content safety and moderation. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Appeals, escalation, and human review
items.text: Use appeals, escalation, and human review to reason about behavior under real workloads, not just a successful local example. Measure latency and cost on representative requests, define operational limits and rollback options, and test what happens when dependencies slow down or fail.

content_blocks.title: Provider and version note
content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice content policy design within content safety and moderation: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.

summary: Content Safety and Moderation is one part of a larger generative AI application lifecycle.
Use explicit inputs, criteria, and reproducible examples to test the concept.
Document uncertainty, failure modes, security considerations, and version assumptions.
